title: Pushing to a remote
idea: A remote is another copy of your repository, usually on a server such as GitHub. `git push` uploads your new commits to it.

analogy.text: Pushing is like adding pages to a shared binder. The binder refuses new pages until you have read the ones added since your last visit.
analogy.breaks: Everyone holds a full copy, not just a page in the binder.

points: Git stores each remote as a name and URL; `origin` is the usual name.
`git push -u origin main` uploads `main` to `origin` and remembers that link.
`origin/main` records where the remote's `main` was when you last connected.
Rejected? The remote has commits you lack. `git pull` fetches, then merges them.

steps.caption: You commit A. It exists only on your machine, and no remote is involved yet.
`git push -u origin main` uploads A. The `origin/main` label is your record of where the remote stands.
A teammate pushes B. You commit C. Pushing C now would be rejected: the remote has a commit you lack.
`git fetch` downloads B and moves `origin/main`. Your own branch and files do not change.
`git merge origin/main` joins both lines in merge commit M.
`git push` now succeeds: M builds on B, so the remote's `main` moves forward to M.

code.title: Push, rejection, fix
code.caption: Real Git output. A bare repository on disk stands in for GitHub; the commands are the same. Hashes are fixed in this recording.

walk.text: A bare repository holds history but no working files. It stands in for GitHub.
`remote add` stores a name and a URL. `remote -v` lists them.
`-u` records `origin/main` as the branch `main` tracks, so later `git push` needs no arguments.
A teammate clones the remote, commits, and pushes. Clone set up `origin` for them.
You commit too. Your push is rejected: the remote has a commit you lack.
`git fetch` downloads their commit. `status -sb` shows you are ahead and behind. Merge, then push.

pitfalls: Keep access tokens out of the remote URL; Git stores URLs as plain text.
After a rejected push, fetch and merge; `--force` would discard your teammate's commits.
If `git pull` stops about divergent branches, choose: `--no-rebase` merges, `--rebase` rebases.

quiz.q: What does the last command print?
quiz.code:
# main was pushed earlier with -u
git commit --allow-empty -m "More"
git status -sb
quiz.why: `-u` linked `main` to `origin/main`. The new commit exists only locally, so `main` is one commit ahead.

takeaway: A push succeeds only when it moves the remote branch forward.
